essay:
Riverton High should invest its one-time grant in the six-seat creative media space. The deciding question, in my view, is which plan gives students access to something they otherwise could not use at all.

Source B states that the space would let students record podcasts, edit video, and prepare presentations even without equipment at home. That is a resource gap a single grant can close: according to Source C, the full $6,000 would build the recording and editing space, and because the equipment stays at school, any student could book it. Source B also notes that students could learn from each other across subjects, so the space supports presentations in science or history, not only media projects.

The books plan has a strong case. Source A describes requested titles that are unavailable or have long waiting lists, and Source C confirms that the 300 books can be borrowed and used at home. For students without internet at home, that matters. My response is that a waiting list is a problem of quantity, while the lack of recording tools is a problem of having no access at all. Admittedly, that distinction is my own reasoning rather than something the packet measures.

The main weakness of my recommendation is capacity. Six seats and supervised booking will limit use, and the packet gives no estimate of how many students could use the space in a week. The poll does not settle the question either: 72 of 120 voluntary respondents preferred books, but 480 students gave no view at all.

Given these uncertainties, I recommend the media space with a published, school-wide booking schedule and a review after one year to check whether access has been fair.
